column4: God knows the secret and what is still more hidden, closely paralleling 87:7's divine knowledge and anchoring خ ف ي in concealment before the section explores its faint-lightning and rain-expulsion senses.
Abraham names his Lord as the one who created him and guides him, repeating the creation-then-guidance sequence that frames the pasture image.
The same Lord feeds and gives drink, turning creation and guidance in 26:78 toward the nourishment supplied by pasture and rain.
The same Lord causes death and then gives life, stating in personal terms the complete transition that the section watches in soil and grass.
Gardens of palms and grapes and flowing springs continue 36:33's revived dead earth, showing the abundant living form reached after grain is brought out.
Worldly enjoyment is set against what is with God as better and more lasting, directly stating the value contrast that the section makes visible through transient grass.
Everything upon the earth is perishing, extending the pasture's short life into a universal statement about the earthly scene.
The face of the majestic and generous Lord remains after all earthly things perish, supplying the enduring pole opposite 55:26 and the section's decaying vegetation.
“You love the immediate life” repeats the human preference voiced in 87:16, while the section's plant cycle shows why that preference is misplaced.
“You leave the Hereafter” supplies the neglected counterpart to 75:20, matching the section's turn from the lower life to what is better and more lasting.
People love the immediate life and leave a weighty day behind them, another direct formulation of the stance that the pasture's rapid decay exposes.
A lush garden of palms, vines, fruits, and rivers is struck by a fiery whirlwind and burned when its owner is vulnerable, sharply reversing sustained green provision into sudden ruin.
People seeing a fragment of sky falling call it a piled cloud, a contrary cloud-recognition scene that echoes the first appearance of cloud while exposing refusal to recognize impending destruction.
Livestock and cultivated fields appear among the adorned desires of worldly life, joining the pasture's animal-and-plant world to the lower life's attraction.
Abundant rain and flowing rivers accompany the establishment of earlier generations before those generations are destroyed, placing heavenly provision and human transience in one historical cycle.
Gardens, palms, and crops of differing produce are followed by the command to eat at fruiting and give their due at harvest, extending the section's plant lifetime into ripening and reaping.
Salih's she-camel is to be left to eat on God's earth, repeating the animal-side realization of pasture as grazing.
The addressees are asked whether they are content with worldly life instead of the Hereafter and are told its enjoyment is slight, closely restating 87:16–17 without the plant simile.
The sky is promised as abundant rain that adds strength, presenting rain as sustained divine provision rather than naming the vegetation it produces.
Livestock are beautiful when brought home and when sent out to pasture, supplying the daily herd movement implicit in المرعى's grazing sense.
The Hour is said to be nearly concealed, a primary concealment use of خ ف ي that helps mark the semantic distance to the section's weak flash at a cloud edge.

Moses says knowledge of former generations is with his Lord in a record and that his Lord neither errs nor forgets, joining Rabb, hidden knowledge, and the no-forgetting context near the quoted Moses passage.
The magicians declare God better and more lasting after rejecting Pharaoh's temporal coercion, another lived choice of the enduring over the nearer power.
The tree from Sinai grows bearing oil and food, continuing the measured rain and gardens of 23:18–19 with a particular nourishing plant.
Human life is compressed from dust through infancy, maturity, old age, and death, a non-botanical parallel to the whole lifespan compressed into the section's two plant ayat.
Tall palms with layered clusters stand between blessed rain in 50:9 and provision and revival in 50:11, contributing the passage's most visibly upright growth.
A violent wind leaves people like uprooted palm trunks, another transfer of ruined vegetation imagery to a destroyed people beside the section's غثاء comparison.
Abundant fruit in the garden supplies a flourishing vegetal counter-scene to the pasture's quick exhaustion.
The fruit is neither cut off nor withheld, making unending plant provision a specific contrast to grass that dries and is swept away.
After the relentless wind, people lie like hollow fallen palm trunks, repeating the image of human destruction as plant wreckage.

One received image compares the fire's sparks to yellow camels; it may recall the section's secondary definition of an أَحْوَىٰ camel as carrying yellow with darker color, but the word is also understood through a rope-like image and no pasture appears.
